A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same research work. Their complete text, equations, tables, figures, and appendices are readable and support comparison despite substantial revisions.

before.justification: v1 reports original tool-use experiments, alignment comparisons, and hallucination analyses in Tables 1–3.

after.justification: v2 reports original model comparisons, scaling experiments, and a human evaluation of hallucination detection in Appendix A.

M1.justification: v1 constructs DPO preferences between trajectories ranked by task outcome and hallucination rate. v2 instead specifies step-level sampling and preference pairs ordered as correct calls, indecisive actions, and hallucinated calls. This substantively revises preference construction; the ChangeTools and TalkToUser actions and sequential SFT–DPO training remain.

E1.justification: Missing-parameter and unmatched-tool scenarios already exist in v1. v2 names the collection RelyToolBench and adds evaluations on I2 Category and I3 Instruction partitions. However, the PDFs do not adequately describe these partitions' task requirements or tool populations to distinguish new coverage from additional splits within retained coverage.

E2.justification: v2 adds evaluated RLHF and StepTool comparisons, plus GPT-4o-mini and GPT-4o alongside GPT-3.5. Table 2 also expands model comparisons to ToolLLaMA 7B and Qwen2.5, beyond the Llama3.1-based alignment experiments in v1.

E3.justification: The reported evaluator changes from GPT-4o-mini to GPT-4o, and Llama3.1 baseline fine-tuning changes from the full ToolBench training set to 5,000 samples. v2 adds data-size and model-size evaluation protocols and a 150-case human check. It also removes benefit-cost ratio from evaluation and rewrites the utility formula.

E4.justification: v2 adds original-versus-reliable pass-rate analysis, training-data scaling from 1k to 5k, model scaling from 1.5B to 14B, human detector validation, and a missing-parameter case study. These investigate new questions beyond v1's training-variant comparisons and hallucination-type breakdown.

E5.justification: Neither version reports experimental seeds, repeated-run counts, confidence intervals, significance tests, or error bars. The new human-validation counts describe sampled cases, not repeated-run or uncertainty reporting.

E6.justification: Results are extensively replaced and expanded. v1's sequential SFT–DPO reports overall RePR 69.2% and tool hallucination 18.8%; v2's Llama3.1+Relign reports 77.2% and 14.6%. Changed methods, training, evaluators, and test partitions prevent interpreting this as a same-setting gain. New results include 139/150 correct detector classifications; benefit-cost-ratio results are removed.

T1.justification: v2 introduces a formal step-level action preference hierarchy in place of v1's within-outcome trajectory ranking. It removes the benefit-cost-ratio and associated cost definitions and rewrites utility with a separate hallucination penalty. The rewritten equation subtracts a penalty specified as negative, creating a sign inconsistency. Neither version contains substantive proofs.

C1.justification: v2 promotes RelyToolBench construction and RePR to explicit contributions, replacing v1's emphasis on StableToolBench evaluation and benefit-cost ratio. RePR itself already appears in v1. The central claims about hallucination categorization and reliability alignment through indecisive actions remain.

C2.justification: v2 adds explanations involving possible overfitting, sequential dependencies, and model capacity, while removing v1's explicit model-size and benchmark limitations. Its new claim that larger models reduce both tool and task hallucination conflicts with Figure 8, whose task-hallucination curve rises overall.

D1.justification: v2 newly documents dataset counts, single-tool SFT sample selection, ten DPO candidates per step, and retaining one sample per preference combination. It adds a future code/data release promise without an access link. Core hyperparameters, A800 hardware, and the five appendix prompts' instructions remain.

R1.justification: v2 adds references including StepTool, Qwen2.5, and MetaGPT, and explicitly positions Relign against existing tool-learning reward methods. Most of the related-work discussion and its distinction from earlier hallucination research remain substantively unchanged.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, and method narrative are extensively rewritten. Metric and dataset sections are reorganized, benchmark construction receives its own section, and experimental discussion is restructured. The author list changes, the framework gains the Relign name, and the appendices are reorganized around retained prompts and new evaluations.

P2.justification: v2 introduces a system diagram, metric-comparison plots, scaling plots, and a case-study figure. Main results are consolidated into a larger table grouped by model, and the hallucination-type table becomes a stacked-bar figure. Figure 1 is reformatted, and the document template and appendix layouts change substantially.

improvement.justification: Additional model families, relevant RLHF/StepTool controls, and Appendix A's human validation strengthen the empirical support beyond v1's narrow comparisons and unvalidated detector. However, the new utility sign inconsistency, the Figure 8 interpretation contradicting its plotted results, and removal of explicit limitations weaken precision and transparency. These tradeoffs limit the net quality improvement.
